top_comments: It’s a long article, and the most important idea is buried towards the end:> That’s where I come back to the idea of mechanism design as reverse game theory. Rather than asking ourselves the rules of the game we are now playing, it calls us to ask “What game ought we to be playing?” And that question leads me imperatively to my answer: “The game of human flourishing.”I wholeheartedly agree: we should think way harder about what we want humanity to optimize for collectively, rather than keeping it haphazard.The current economic system is built on the idea of ‘shareholder value maximisation’, which, in a finite world, will ultimately become simply ‘value extraction’. With AI, we’ve built an automated value extractor, which can extract value even faster than was done before. Because of that, the old model can no longer work for improving human flourishing — in a finite world, it will inevitably lead to economic accumulation by few entities, throttling the economic flow.

Attempts at governance are futile until we recognize that we have built a machine and set it on its course. Instead, we pretend that the market is a natural phenomenon best left alone, and we fail to hold its mechanism designers to account. We need to tear down and rebuild that machine, reprogramming it so that human flourishing, not corporate profit, becomes its goal.This article has useful insights. It points out that capitalism is an optimization engine for something. Shareholder value and CEO compensation, mostly. It reminds us of something that many people would prefer be forgotten - capitalism operates under rules set by governments, and those shape the market. Tax law matters - what's deductible warps spending patterns. Bankruptcy law matters - who gets left holding the bag? Corporation law matters - how immune are executives from the consequences of their decisions? Labor law matters - do people go to jail for wage and hour law violations?All of those are changeable by legislation. Most have become much more favorable to companies since 1970. That's not necessarily permanent. We had a New Deal in the 1930s, following the Gilded Age of the 1920s and the crash of 1929.

I don't disagree with anything O'Reilly is saying but lets also call out the proximate cause which is that ZIRP era allowed these companies to grow to grotesque proportions and incentivized upstarts to shoot big in green fields rather than compete in known markets. Now interest rates are back and tech companies are cannibalizing their core competencies on the back of AI. Will markets begin slapping wrists for reckless spending and will upstarts see weakness and stab at exposed bellies? No guarantee they will but it is more possible than analysts are realizing.

Perplexity is not defined in the article. FYI:Perplexity is the degree of surprise the model has in predicting the next token, over a sequence of tokens. At the worst case, perplexity is equal to the size of the vocabulary. At the best case, perplexity is 1.So, given a sequence of tokens, "e = m c ^ 2", if the p(token | prev tokens) = 1 for every token, perplexity ends up being 1. If, however, it's a random predictor, the p(token | prev tokens) is 1/vocab for every token, and perplexity ends up being len(vocab).The article plots log(perplexity) on the y-axis, which puts the best case at 0 (i.e. log 1).

This trend is pretty shocking to me. I assumed that we had moved beyond cross-entropy loss being important with the increasing use of RL, it's wild that the trend is so clear. Really nice to have such a simple benchmark instead of the increasingly convoluted ones that are getting spun up every day.Also, I wonder what happened with GPT 4.5? I think o1 was the start of true reasoning models, right? I was using Claude at the time so I can't remember.

The perplexity / intelligence correspondence is one of those ideas that is surprising at first, but in retrospect could not work any other way. The "magic" of intelligence is the ability to extract sophisticated world models from large volumes of raw sensor data. The prediction (=compression) rate on the raw data stream is exactly the metric that captures this progress.I argued this point in a 2008 paper: https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-540-69134-1_...I elaborated on this idea in my 2011 book: https://arxiv.org/abs/1104.5466I used the word "reusability" to express the idea that the world models obtained via the large scale data compression task could be repurposed for other tasks.(So, Burfoot, if you were so prescient, why aren't you a rich and famous frontier lab researcher? The answer is: I did not think neural nets would scale up).

articles.title: The Birds of GTA 6: A Field Guide to Vice City and Leonida's Wildlife
articles.summary: The Birds of GTA 6: A Field Guide to Vice City and Leonida's Wildlife

top_comments: Why do the animations of the seagulls taking off bother me? It looks all the same and much too fast, like "switched". I love animation and it's clear why all this had started with Dinosaurs of Jurassic Parc: no one knew exactly how real dinosaurs behave and move and so as long as the weight, the force and the noise was there it felt real.Or plastic toys of Toy Story I. Easier to handle and much room for expression. But remember the white dog at the end: A real pain to watch. I feel very sorry for the person who had to do this. At least they finally made up for it with the very impressive cat in IV. Nearly better than real.Starting birds are also very observable, but maybe even harder to animate. Each species is very unique and endlessly interesting. Some are playful, some start straight, and some take-offs are very spectacular: watch a starting swan from a lake. This seemingly endless 20, 30, 40 seconds of acceleration, heavy wings flapping, desperate feet running-flapping on the water and finally the mass of the bird is airborne!I know a bit animation-master and houdini, and think that the tools to build the correct animations in the first place are still either quite limited or heavily overcomplex, let alone to transfer these into reusable blendable formats working for many ingame situations.For me, the movement of a starting bird is something sacred and deserves every least bit of attention.

While we are commenting on anything but the birds: I really wish games like this had some kind of co-play available. Would seem to fit the narrative to have one partner play Jason and the other play Lucia (or some otherwise NPC friend when they are apart). It would make it much more engaging to play with family/ friendsFor context, I just bought this and have been passing the controller back and forth with my adult son all weekend

The game appears to be mostly story/character focused rather than sandbox focused, despite the insane attention to detail on traditional sandbox elements (for context, I've already completed the main campaign). In a lot of ways it feels like two disjoint teams worked to create the final product and the story/character team won out. Not sure if that's ultimately the root cause of the stated inconsistencies, but it could be a contributing factor.

articles.title: A Beginner's Guide to Local AI with Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth
articles.summary: A Beginner's Guide to Local AI with Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth

top_comments: This is the plasma TV phase of local AI.Early, heavy and priced premium. I estimate it will take ~5 years for most practical AI to run on our own machines, with a few super brains left in the cloud.I have been putting some effort into making local AI as consumer friendly as possible on macOS with this project https://github.com/pdparchitect/noodle/ but I will be the first to admit that the hardware you need is beyond most people's budgets. Hell, perhaps beyond most enterprises comfort levels too.For now, subscriptions are the most practical way in.

The Nvidia P40 is a good way to play with local AI while not spending thousands of dollars.The card goes for about 300 USD on Ebay and it gives you 24GB of GDDR5. See this for the particulars of setting it up because it's not quite plug and play.https://github.com/JingShing/How-to-use-tesla-p40I'm running Qwen 3.8 27B UD-Q4_K_M at 14t/s with llama.cpp on Ubuntu and it's very useful, not just a toy.

Since Spring, I've been working on a locally hosted, containerized web application to narrate my audiobook using a full cast of characters (skip to 9m47s for a reading of the demo book):https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Q9PKT6bdKncAll weights are either permissively licensed or free until fantasy-level monthly recurring revenue sets in. The system runs entirely on the following hardware: CPU: AMD Ryzen 5 7600 (Zen 4), 6 cores / 12 threads, AVX-512 GPU: NVIDIA T1000, 8 GB GDDR6 (Turing, 896 CUDA cores, 50 W, no BF16) RAM: 96 GB DDR5 Text analysis uses Qwen3.6-35B-A3B MTP (Q4_K_XL GGUF) for speaker attribution, voice descriptions (not voice audio), emotive directions, and grammar. Both Muse Glimmer and GRMR cannot compete with Qwen3.6 for grammar checking. I haven't tried Gemma4, but I suspect Qwen3.6 remains the champ. My hope is that Inkling is more accurate for grammar than Qwen3.6, which is being tested at time of writing.Voice design and cloning uses FireRedTTS3, OmniVoice, Qwen3-TTS, VoxCPM2, and Ming-3.0-tts-tiny. Most are approximately equivalent. For narration, nothing comes close to Drama 3 Expressive Medium fine-tune in terms of quality, consistency, or pacing.Unsloth's GGUFs have been absolutely instrumental in making the system a reality. Highly recommend using them.

articles.summary: Free alternative TV network built from the Internet Archive's forgotten videos

top_comments: For me the allure of TV is its topicality. Who wants yesterdays papers? I know some do but I want the feeling that I am learning something about what is in the world right now.

Before streaming, your only option was cable, so watching TV was an appointment, a time and a place where you had to arrive, or you'd miss a show. The same thing can be said about the internet; your computer was a desktop tethered to the wall. It was a specific place you had to go.Now, the internet and streaming and TV is accessible at the touch of a screen, 24/7. We have unmatched convenience today, but the price of that is an unhealthy relationship with our media and devices, and more than a few social crises.
I think I'd want the original air date of everything, on the website.

articles.title: Progress map for the Lean formalization of Alessandro Masullo's manuscript
articles.summary: Progress map for the Lean formalization of Alessandro Masullo's manuscript

top_comments: I'm one of the mathematicians actually contributing to this repo, just a few things:1. If you have some tokens to spare we are happy if you point your agent at this project. https://github.com/mccorvie/riemann-masullo/blob/main/CONTRI...2. Do not read to much into the list of hundreds of issues found in the errata. Some are minor some are not so minor, it is way too early to tell if there is a big hole in the core of the idea or not. A lot of these hunderds of issues have been fixed. Some need more attention, probably even from Masullo himself. Math used to be a subject area that required a lot of patience, and I hope that people will still have some of this left.3: My main goal for contributing to the repository is to formalise as much as possible in the repository so that it is clear which statements in the paper are true beyond doubt. And in doing so hopefully give Masullo some firmer ground to stand on in completing the actual hard parts. And to give him some support now the entire world is criticizing is forced premature publication of a draft in a science that used to be about slow and steady wins the race. And from one day to the next suddenly got taken over by move fast and break things mentality.

The professor who originally posted this claim (Ravi Vakil, on behalf of Masullo) now claims he has not even looked at Masullo's document (see bottom of http://math216.wordpress.com/2026/11/20/hurried-announcement...)Upon inquiry from Scientific American, Brian Conrad, the only professor who seems to be vouching for this claim, says the manuscript needs "major revision".Alessandro Masullo has no other publications besides this alleged proof, other than his thesis (also with Brian Conrad). He is not otherwise widely known in the math community.Besides the timing, there is no reason to give this claim any more attention than there is for any of the other unsuccessful claims to a proof, of which there are many: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_hypothesis#Attempted_pr...

Just a reminder not to take the progress bar here as an indication that the proof is largely correct, as it takes only one hole for the entire thing to come crashing down.Judging by other commentary so far, my understanding is that there is a major hole in this proof, which would not surprise me given that the machinery involved feels far less like a major leap (to me anyway) than the route for the Alpoge proof. The asymptotic-order theta lifting in that proof feels like a genuine step forward for other mathematical disciplines. But I'm not a number theorist, so happy for someone else to pitch in and correct me.
